title: API Design
overview: This topic covers how to design, version, secure and operate APIs well. It starts with treating APIs as products and the design principles behind them, then covers REST constraints, resource and HTTP method best practices, the Richardson Maturity Model and GraphQL as an alternative. It moves on to versioning, OAuth-based security, resilience and testing, and distributed transactions across microservices. For the exam, expect to design or critique an API for a scenario and justify style, versioning and security choices.
big_ideas: Manage APIs as a **product**: outside-in, data-driven, MVP first, success measured by adoption.
REST has six constraints: client-server, stateless, uniform interface, layered, caching and optional code on demand. Stateless requests simplify scaling; resource data remains on the server.
Resources are plural kebab-case nouns; path identifies, query params filter/sort/paginate; verbs carry the action.
Safe methods request no business-state change. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST and PATCH are not guaranteed idempotent.
Richardson Maturity Model: 0 one endpoint, 1 resources, 2 HTTP verbs, 3 hypermedia (HATEOAS).
GraphQL lets clients select fields through a typed schema, often reducing round trips; REST fits resource-oriented APIs and standard HTTP caching.
Version with MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH via URI or header; never remove or change meaning abruptly.
Across microservices use SAGA (events plus compensation) or two-phase commit instead of a single DB transaction.

sections.title: API as a product and design principles
sections.summary: Treat an API as an ongoing product: design for consumers, measure adoption and keep its contract useful and stable.

items: **APIs contribute to revenue** → lecture examples: Salesforce, eBay, Expedia
**Adoption and usage data** guide improvements
**Outside-in**: design from the needs of consuming developers and end users
**Inside-out** (avoid): design from whatever internal resources happen to exist
**Reach developers** through forums and conferences
**Measure success** by adoption and business impact
**Launch an MVP**
**Mature the API** through iterations, feedback and backlog grooming
**Easy to discover**: APIs must also be discoverable

sub: design at the lowest practical level so APIs can be recombined
apply the **Single Responsibility** and **Interface Segregation** principles
explicit service levels for A/B versions

terms.def: Designing APIs around consumer and end-user needs rather than exposing existing internal resources.
Role accountable for the API as a product: usage, adoption, roadmap and stakeholder needs.
Single Responsibility and Interface Segregation: small, focused APIs that consumers can combine.

check.q: A bank exposes each table of its core system as its own API and calls the job done. Six months later almost nobody uses them. Diagnose the problem.

a.lead: **Inside-out design**: the APIs expose existing resources rather than what consumers need → developers find them hard to use or not useful.
items: **Outside-in strategy**: start from the needs of developers and end users
Launch an **MVP**
Measure success by **adoption** and **business impact** through **usage analytics**
**API as a product**: the bank should treat the APIs as a product with an **owner** who iterates on that feedback

check.q: An API team is disbanded the week after launch because 'the project is delivered'. What goes wrong over the next year?

items: Nobody acts on **usage analytics** or **developer feedback** → the API **stops improving**
**Versions**, **documentation** and **endpoint stability** no longer managed → consumers meet **breaking changes** and **stale docs**
a.foot: The lecture's point: manage APIs as **products, not projects**: a **product owner** keeps a **backlog** from feedback and matures the API through **iterations**.

check.q: A single endpoint, /process-customer, creates a customer, opens an account and sends a welcome pack in one call. A partner only needs to create customers. Critique the design.

a.lead: Breaks the **granularity principles**: one API with several responsibilities.
items: Forces the partner to depend on behaviour it does not use → against **single responsibility** and **interface segregation**
**Design at the lowest practical level**: separate **customer** and **account** resources → consumers can combine them in different ways
a.foot: Trade-off: clients that need all three steps now make **more calls**, which a **composite at the gateway** can hide if needed.

check.q: A platform publishes its API with only a Java SDK and a custom binary protocol. Which design principle does this break, and what would you change?

a.lead: Breaks **ubiquitous standards**: develop APIs on **well-accepted standards** and make **no assumptions about the consumer's technology**.
items: Custom protocol + one SDK → **excludes consumers** on other stacks and slows **adoption**
**Fix**: expose a standard protocol such as **HTTP with JSON** and maintain **SDKs for several technologies**
a.foot: Cost: more SDKs to maintain.

sections.title: API styles and the REST constraints
sections.summary: A quick map of the main API styles, then the six REST constraints (client-server, stateless, uniform interface, layered, caching, code on demand) and why each helps scale.

items: **SOAP** → enterprise integration (example in the lecture)
**REST** → exposes web resources
**GraphQL** → changing field requirements
**gRPC** → low-latency service calls
**WebSocket** → continuous two-way communication
**Webhooks** → notify a registered URL of events
notes.foot: **Security** still needs deliberate design for every style.

items: **Client-server**
**Stateless**
**Uniform interface**
**Layered architecture**
**Caching**
**Code-on-demand** → the only optional one
notes.foot: All the others are required for a service to be called **RESTful**.

items: **Each request carries the context** needed to process it
**No stored client session**: the server does not rely on earlier requests
**Any suitable instance** can handle it → simplifies **load balancing**
**Persistent resource data** still lives on the server
**Cacheability** depends on response semantics and headers
**Resources have URIs**
**Self-descriptive messages**
**Representations**: clients manipulate resources through them
**Hypermedia links** describe next actions

sub: the verb is not part of the URI

notes.lead: Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State
items: **Responses carry links**
**Server drives** application state and URL structure
**Clients discover and navigate** the API by following links
→ **loose coupling**
**Layered architecture**: a client may reach the API through a gateway or load balancer
**Shared cache pros**: reduces separate per-instance copies; survives application restarts
**Shared cache cons**: adds network latency and operating cost
**Consistency and durability** of caches depend on configuration
**Server extends the client** by sending scripts or applets
→ fewer features need pre-implementing in the client

terms.def: Each request carries all context; the server stores no client application state between calls.
Hypermedia links in responses tell the client what it can do next, so the server drives navigation.
The only optional REST constraint: server sends executable code to extend the client.
Event-driven callback: the server calls a URL you registered when something happens.

check.q: An API keeps each user's session in the memory of the instance that served the login, so the load balancer uses sticky sessions. Traffic triples during a sale and one instance crashes. What goes wrong, and what does REST's stateless constraint suggest?

items: **Sessions lost**: users pinned to the crashed instance lose their sessions
**Uneven load**: requests must return to their own instance → load cannot be spread evenly
**Statelessness**: the **client holds the application state** and **each request carries its own context**
→ **any instance can serve any request** → scale by **adding instances**, with no server-side **session synchronisation**
a.foot: Persistent resource data still needs a **shared store**.

check.q: An API runs on eight instances, each with an in-process cache of product prices. Users see different prices depending on which instance answers. Diagnose the problem and propose a fix.

a.lead: Each **in-process cache is local to its instance** → updates reach the caches at different times.
items: **Fix: distributed cache** → consistent across requests to multiple servers
Survives **restarts and deployments**
a.foot: Trade-off: **slower than local memory**, another service to run, and still needs a policy for **invalidating stale entries**.

check.q: Pick an API style for (a) in-app chat, (b) telling a partner system the moment a file upload completes, and (c) a mobile dashboard whose data needs vary by screen. Justify each choice.

items: **(a) WebSocket**: continuous **two-way real-time** messages
**(b) Webhook**: an **event notification** that calls the partner when the upload happens → the partner does not have to **poll**
**(c) GraphQL**: each screen asks for **exactly the fields** it needs in **one request**
a.foot: These match the lecture's typical uses; a **REST** API could still serve (c) if **HTTP caching** matters more than flexible queries.

check.q: A reviewer says your API is not RESTful because the server never sends scripts for the client to run. Do you agree?

a.lead: **No.** **Code on demand** is the one REST constraint that is **not strictly required**.
items: It lets the server **extend a client by sending code** → reduces what the client must pre-implement
**Required constraints**: **client-server**, **stateless**, **uniform interface**, **layered system**, **caching**
a.foot: Review the API against the required ones instead.

items.label: SOAP
items.detail: The lecture’s example is security-heavy banking integration. The protocol choice does not replace authentication, authorisation and transport security.

items.label: REST
items.detail: Web applications and services where scalability and flexibility are key, such as social media APIs.

items.label: GraphQL
items.detail: Complex applications with dynamic data requirements, such as data-driven dashboards or mobile apps.

items.label: gRPC
items.detail: Microservices, real-time systems and low-latency applications like IoT or gaming servers.

items.label: WebSocket
items.detail: Real-time applications like chat systems, live updates or online multiplayer games.

items.label: Webhook
items.detail: Automation tasks and event notifications, such as triggering events when a file is uploaded.

sections.title: Resource naming, HTTP methods and idempotency
sections.summary: Practical rules for URI design and for choosing HTTP methods, with the safe/idempotent distinction and how to keep payment-style calls from duplicating.

items: **Nouns, not verbs**: /customers, not /getCustomers
**Plural nouns** (exception: singleton sub-resources like /customers/{id}/address)
**kebab-case** for multi-word names: /order-items
**No trailing slash**, for consistency

items.t: **Query parameters** (belong in the query string) → shaping

notes.foot: Paths identify a resource; query parameters adjust how it is returned.

items: **GET** → retrieve
**POST** → create new resources and sub-resources
**PUT** → update/replace an existing resource
**PATCH** → partial update
**DELETE** → remove
**PUT** → sets the representation at a known URI; may create there if the contract permits
**POST** → submits data to a collection or operation; often creating a server-assigned resource
**Idempotency**: PUT is idempotent; POST is not guaranteed to be
**PATCH** → expresses a partial change
**POST caching** needs explicit cache semantics and suitable cache support
**Safe** = does not request a business-state change → GET, HEAD, OPTIONS (incidental logging is compatible with safety)
**Idempotent** = repeats have the same intended effect as one request
**PUT, DELETE** → idempotent but not safe
**POST, PATCH** → not guaranteed idempotent
**DELETE may return 204 then 404** → without changing that property (still idempotent)
**One unique idempotency key** per intended payment
**Reuse that same key** on retries
**Server records the outcome** and recognises repeats → prevents duplicate charges
notes.foot: Implements the goal in the lecture of **preventing duplicate transactions**.

sub: headers (client type, accepted formats, cache settings)

terms.def: Repeating the request produces the same resulting state as sending it once.
A method that does not request a business-state change; GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are safe.
Path identifies the resource; query parameters filter, sort or paginate it.

check.q: Critique this orders API and rewrite it: POST /createOrder; GET /orders/delete?id=9; PUT /orders with the new order in the body; GET /getCustomers?customer-id=7&orders-id=9; GET /products/sort/price/page/2.

items: **Plural nouns, no verbs**: POST /orders to create (**201**)
**GET must be safe** → deletion becomes DELETE /orders/9
**PUT updates a known resource** → PUT /orders/9 or PATCH /orders/9
**Path variables** for identity and relationships → GET /customers/7/orders/9
**Query parameters** only to shape results → GET /products?sort=price&page=2&limit=50
a.lead: Resources should be plural nouns; fix each call:

check.q: A mobile client times out on POST /payments and retries. How do you make sure the customer is not charged twice?

items: **Idempotency key**: generate one for the intended payment and send the **same key on every retry**
Server **records the key with the outcome** → on a repeat, returns the **recorded result** without charging again
a.foot: Pitfalls: generating a **fresh key per attempt** defeats the protection; the server must **keep keys** long enough to cover the **retry window**.

check.q: A client times out on DELETE /orders/9, retries, and gets 404. A developer fears the retry did harm. Did it?

a.lead: **No.** **DELETE is idempotent**.
items: **Idempotency concerns server state**: after one or several calls the order is gone either way
Only the **response** differs: typically **204** then **404**
a.foot: The client should treat a **404 on a retried delete** as 'already deleted'.

check.q: A cart API offers PATCH /carts/5/items/3 with either {"quantity": 5} or {"increment": 1}. The client library retries PATCH automatically on timeout. Is that safe?

a.lead: **Only for the first form.**
items: **Setting quantity to 5**: leaves the **same state** however often it repeats
**Incrementing by 1**: adds **another item on every retry**
**PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent**
a.foot: Fix: either disable **automatic retries** for the increment or protect it with an **idempotency key**.

sections.title: Meaningful responses and status codes
sections.summary: Return the right status class and examples so developers can succeed, and debug a production 500 methodically rather than by changing code blindly.

notes.h: Tell the client who is at fault
items: **2xx** → client and API worked
**4xx** → client erred; should change the request
**5xx** → the API erred
notes.foot: Good feedback and examples improve **developer experience**, speed up documentation and raise **adoption**.

items: **200 OK** → often GET
**201 Created** → after a create, usually POST
**204 No Content** → usually PUT/PATCH
**400 Bad Request**
**401 Unauthorized** → credentials not recognised
**403 Forbidden** → credentials accepted but no permission
**404 Not Found**
**500 Internal Server Error** → generic
**503 Service Unavailable** → retry headers are useful
**401** → we do not know who you are
**403** → we know you, but you may not do this

notes.lead: Posed as a question in the lecture; the method is standard practice.
items: **Never change code randomly** in production
**Find the cause first** → logs, metrics and traces

terms.def: Client error: the request was wrong; client should modify it.
Server error: the API or backend failed.
Unauthenticated versus authenticated but not permitted.

check.q: An API returns 200 with the body {"error": "customer not found"} for unknown customers, and 500 when the client sends malformed JSON. What is wrong, and what should it return?

a.lead: Return **404** for the missing customer and **400** for the malformed request.
items: **Status codes tell the developer who behaved wrongly**: **4xx** = the client did, **5xx** = the API did
**As built**: clients cannot handle errors from the status code
**Monitoring** raises server alarms for client mistakes while **missing real failures**

check.q: A clerk with a valid token calls DELETE /accounts/7, which only managers may do, and the API returns 401. Is that the right code?

a.lead: **No, it should be 403**: the credentials were accepted, but the caller **lacks permission** for this resource.
items: **401** = credentials **missing or not recognised** → the client may try to **log in again**, which cannot help
**Clear codes** improve **developer experience** → API easier to **adopt**

check.q: Since this morning's release, 2% of requests return 500. A developer proposes changing code directly on a production server to test a theory. How do you respond?

a.lead: **Don't**: blind changes in production are the lecture's **'big mistake'** → they can **widen the outage** and leave **no audit trail**.
items: **Correlate logs, metrics and traces** to find the failing path
**Compare** against what the release changed, and **reproduce safely**
If the release is the cause → **roll back**, then ship a **verified fix** through the **normal pipeline**

check.q: A downstream dependency is down for planned maintenance for ten minutes. Should your API answer 500 or 503?

a.lead: **503 Service Unavailable**, ideally with a **retry header**.
items: **503** → tells clients the condition is **temporary**; a later retry may succeed
**500** = **generic server error** → invites **investigation** rather than a timed retry
a.foot: Clients still need **backoff** so they do not hammer the API when it comes back.

sections.title: Richardson Maturity Model
sections.summary: RMM separates resource identification, HTTP semantics and hypermedia into levels 0–3. It describes API design, not a throughput measurement.

items: **Level 1** → resources
**Level 2** → HTTP methods and status codes
**Level 3** → hypermedia
**Can improve** interoperability and evolution
**Not a performance guarantee**: a higher level does not by itself guarantee lower latency or higher capacity

sub: HTTP is only a transport to a single endpoint
analogy: one takeaway serves everything; you order pizza, rice and curry from it
separate resources get their own URIs
but a single HTTP method is used
analogy: visit different restaurants per dish
resource nouns + proper verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and status codes
analogy: change toppings at the pizza place, cancel at another
minimum the workshop asks for (Level 2 or 3)
the response tells you what you ordered, what other options exist and links to more information

terms.def: Richardson Maturity Model: levels 0-3 measuring adoption of REST ideas.
Plain Old XML; level 0, HTTP used as a tunnel to one endpoint.

check.q: A booking API has one endpoint, POST /api, with bodies such as {"action": "getBooking", "id": 5} and {"action": "cancelBooking", "id": 5}. Which RMM level is it, and what changes would take it to level 2?

a.lead: **Level 0**: HTTP is only a **transport for RPC-style messages** → no resources and no HTTP semantics.
items: **Level 1**: each booking gets its own **URI**, /bookings/5

items.t: **Level 2**: then use the **verbs** and **status codes** properly
sub: **Cancel**: DELETE /bookings/5, or a **PATCH** of its status (**204**)

check.q: An API exposes GET /v1/rooms/{room-id} to read a room and GET /v1/rooms/{room-id}/book to make a booking. The team says it is level 2 because it has resources. Do you agree?

a.lead: **No**: it has resource URIs, which is only **level 1**.
items: Uses **GET for a state-changing action** and puts a **verb in the path** → does not use HTTP verbs as **level 2** requires
**GET must be safe**: caches, crawlers or retries could **create bookings by accident**
**Fix**: model bookings as a resource → POST /v1/rooms/{room-id}/bookings returning **201** with the new booking's **location**

check.q: A mobile client hard-codes 40 URL patterns and breaks whenever the server reorganises its URLs. Which RMM level addresses this, and what does it demand of the client?

a.lead: **Level 3, HATEOAS.**
items: Responses carry **hypermedia links** to related resources and next actions
→ the **server controls URL structure**; the client **discovers** it from responses
→ **looser coupling**; lets the API **evolve**
a.foot: Demand on the client: it must be written to **follow links instead of building URLs**, and responses get somewhat **larger**.

check.q: A teammate says moving the API from RMM level 2 to level 3 will raise its throughput under load. Do you agree?

a.lead: **Not as stated.**
items: **RMM grades** how fully an API uses **resources**, **HTTP semantics** and **hypermedia**
The lecture links higher levels with **scalability** and **evolvability** through **looser coupling** and **cacheable, uniform interfaces**
But **adding links** does not by itself make requests **faster**
a.foot: **Throughput** has to be shown with **load tests**.

layers.label: Level 3: Hypermedia
layers.detail: Responses include links telling the client what it can do next; server directs application state.

layers.label: Level 2: HTTP verbs
layers.detail: Full use of all HTTP verbs combined with resource nouns.

layers.label: Level 1: Resources
layers.detail: Distinguishes between resources but uses one HTTP method.

layers.label: Level 0: POX
layers.detail: HTTP is only transport and does not indicate application state, like classic SOAP and XML-RPC.

sections.title: GraphQL vs REST and API documentation standards
sections.summary: GraphQL as a client-driven alternative to REST, how it works, when each wins, and the specification formats used to document APIs.

items: **Query language and runtime**: clients select fields from a server-defined schema
**One query, one endpoint** → customer, order and product data together
→ reduces client **round trips** and unwanted fields
**Server still performs** the underlying data access

sub: **resolvers** → functions that turn an operation into data from a database or legacy API
**GraphiQL** → browser interface to test queries and mutations

items: **Query** → read
**Mutation** → create, update or delete
**Subscription** → live updates
**REST** → create, retrieve, update, delete via HTTP verbs
**GraphQL**: typed field selection → suits changing mobile and dashboard requirements
**REST**: resource endpoints → fit standard HTTP caching, when responses allow it
**GraphQL caching** often needs specialised caching
**Fewer client calls ≠ faster** server execution (not guaranteed)
**OpenAPI** → vendor-neutral API description standard, based on Swagger
**Swagger** → supplies design and documentation tools
**RAML** → machine-readable, human-friendly modelling language
**API Blueprint** → emphasises readable documentation and design before implementation
notes.foot: A **specification** describes the contract; **tools** use it to document or test that contract.

terms.def: Server function that turns a GraphQL operation into data.
Over-fetching returns unwanted fields; under-fetching requires extra requests for missing data.
Vendor-neutral standard description format for REST APIs.

check.q: A mobile screen needs a customer, their last five orders and the product names, which now takes three REST calls over slow networks. Separately, a public product catalogue is read millions of times a day through HTTP caches. Would you use GraphQL for both?

a.lead: **No**: use **GraphQL** for the mobile screen and **REST** for the catalogue.
items: **Mobile screen → GraphQL**: one query to one endpoint returns exactly those fields → avoids **over- and under-fetching** across three calls
**Catalogue → keep REST**: resource URLs and standard **HTTP caching** serve repeated identical reads cheaply
**GraphQL queries are hard to cache** in web caches
a.foot: Cost: running **two styles**, justified by two different **access patterns**.

check.q: A team implements 'place order' as a GraphQL query because the call returns the new order. Critique this.

a.lead: Placing an order **changes data** → it should be a **mutation**; **queries are for reading**.
items: As a query it **misleads clients and tools** that treat queries as **safe to repeat or cache**
→ an **automatic retry** could place a **second order**
**Subscriptions** are the third operation type: **pushing updates** as they happen, such as order status changes

check.q: Team A writes the API code first and generates documentation afterwards. Team B agrees an OpenAPI description with consumers before writing code. What does B's design-first approach buy, and what does it cost?

items: **Separates the interface from the backend implementation** → consumers can **review and build against the contract early**
**Documentation matches the API** from the start
**OpenAPI** is a **vendor-neutral standard format** → tools and consumers on any stack can use it
a.foot: Cost: **upfront agreement time**, and the contract must then be **kept in sync** with the code.

visuals.title: GraphQL vs REST
rows: Can reduce client round trips; resolver work remains
Depends on endpoint shape, caching and call count

sections.title: API versioning and security basics
sections.summary: How to evolve an API without breaking consumers, and the baseline security approach with a gateway, OAuth 2.0 and validation.

items: **Do not take anything away** abruptly
**Do not change the meaning** of an existing API
**Additions are optional**: consumers need not use them
**MAJOR** → breaking changes
**MINOR** → backward-compatible features
**PATCH** → backward-compatible fixes
**URI versioning** → api.example.com/v1; visible and simple

sub: Accept header with a vendor media type: application/vnd.example.v1+json

items: **Validate parameters**
**Threat detection**
**SSL/TLS everywhere**
**Proven solutions**
**Authenticate, then authorise**
**OAuth 2.0** → the industry standard for authorization
**Consolidates API requests** from mobile and web clients
**Interfaces with back-end** microservices or monolith APIs
**Centralises security**
notes.foot: Each back-end service must **still validate requests**.

items: **User approves access** at the authorization server
**App receives a short-lived code**
**Exchanges the code** for an access token
**Presents the token** to the resource API
**API validates** the token and permissions
notes.foot: The API need not contact the authorization server on every call if it can **validate the token locally**.

items: **Rate limiting and quotas**
**HTTP caching headers**
**Circuit breakers and retries**
**Webhooks and callbacks**
**Usage analytics**

terms.def: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH numbering: breaking, feature, fix.
Industry-standard authorization framework issuing access tokens to clients.
Credential the client presents to the resource server instead of the user's password.

check.q: Your API is at version 2.4.1. Give the new version for each change: (a) an optional 'notes' field is added to the order response; (b) 'amount' is renamed to 'total'; (c) a rounding bug is fixed without changing the contract.

items: **(a) 2.5.0**: a backward-compatible feature → bumps the **minor** version
**(b) 3.0.0**: renaming a field **breaks existing consumers** → the **major** version goes up
**(c) 2.4.2**: a backward-compatible fix → bumps the **patch**
a.foot: Change (b) also needs **version 2 kept available** for a while, because the rules say **not to take anything away abruptly**.

check.q: An API puts its full version in every URI, such as /v1.1/orders, and changes the URI for every minor release, so all consumers must update their URLs each time. Propose a better strategy.

a.lead: **Version for breaking changes only.**
items: Put just the **major version** in the URI (/v1/orders) or move it to an **Accept** or **custom header**
Make **minor and patch** releases **backward compatible** → the URIs consumers call stay the same
Keep the **old major version running** with an **explicit service level** while consumers migrate
a.foot: **URI versioning** is visible and easy to test; **header versioning** keeps URIs stable but is harder to see and to try in a browser.

check.q: A field is deprecated and only 3% of calls still use it. The team wants to delete it next week. What do the versioning rules say?

a.lead: **Don't take anything away abruptly.**
items: **Removal is a breaking change** → belongs in a **new major version**
The current version **keeps the field** under an **explicit service level**
The change is **announced** through the **developer portal**
a.foot: The **3%** may include an **important partner**, so check who they are before setting the **deadline**.

check.q: Each of 12 services currently implements its own token validation, rate limits and request validation, each slightly differently. What would you propose, and what must stay in the services?

a.lead: Put an **API gateway** in front as the **single gatekeeper**.
items: → **authentication**, **rate limits** and **schema validation** enforced **consistently** for every client
**Services must still authorise business actions**: a valid token does not prove permission on a particular resource
**Services must still validate the data they rely on**
a.foot: Risk: the gateway becomes a **critical component** and must be **highly available**.

steps.label: User consents
steps.detail: The app asks the user to link to the service; the user logs in and approves the requested permissions.

steps.label: Auth code issued
steps.detail: The authorization server returns a short-lived authorization code to the app.

steps.label: Code for token
steps.detail: The app presents the code to the token endpoint and receives an access token.

steps.label: Call the API
steps.detail: The app presents the access token. The API validates it and checks permissions, using local validation or authorization-server checks as appropriate.

sections.title: Errors, logging, retries, pagination and monitoring
sections.summary: Operational practices that keep an API dependable in production: error handling, logging, resilience patterns, pagination and metrics.

items: **Global exception handling** → stable response format

sub: raise limits only if that payload is legitimate and capacity supports it

items: **Logging gives a trail** of activity before an event
**Supplements exception records**
**Reveals how clients use** the API
**Records metrics**
**e.g.** NLog in .NET Core
**Retry** → transient failures, with bounded exponential backoff
**Timeouts** → bound waiting
**Circuit breaker** → stop calls during persistent failure
**Bulkheads** → isolate resources
**Fallback** → degraded results
notes.foot: Retry only when repeating the operation is **safe or duplicate-protected**.

items: **One API call** can touch multiple services and databases
**Not one atomic transaction** just because it is one call
**Identify partial-failure cases**
**Choose** coordinated commit or compensation where needed
**Offset** → skips a number of rows; may become slow or drift when data changes
**Cursor** → continues from the last position in a stable ordering
**Unique ordering or tie-breaker** → createdOn alone can skip records sharing a timestamp
**Trace the full request** before selecting a fix
**Fast individual queries** do not prove the complete request path is fast

terms.def: Stops calling a failing dependency for a while so failures do not cascade.
Partitioning resources so one failing part cannot exhaust everything.
Page by a stable marker such as last created time instead of a numeric offset.
Retry delays that grow each attempt to avoid overloading a recovering service.

check.q: An activity feed receives new items every second and pages with ?page=N&limit=50. Users scrolling down see duplicate items. Diagnose the problem and fix it.

a.lead: **Offset pagination drifts**: new items inserted at the top push earlier items onto the next page.
items: **Fix: cursor pagination** → ask for items **after the last one seen**
Use a **stable sort order** with a **unique tie-breaker**: a **timestamp alone** can skip or repeat items with equal times
a.foot: Cost: clients can no longer **jump straight to page 37**.

check.q: A client retries every failed call to a slow partner API five times immediately. During a partner outage, the partner receives six times its normal traffic and the client's threads are exhausted. What would you change?

items: **Timeout** → calls cannot wait indefinitely
**Retry with exponential backoff**
**Circuit breaker** in front of the partner → stops calling it after repeated failures and returns a **fallback**
**Bulkhead isolation** → keeps the partner's calls from using up **threads** needed for other work
a.foot: Trade-off: users get **degraded responses** during the outage instead of **eventual success**.

check.q: An operations lead proposes CPU usage as the main health metric for a public API. Does it show what users experience?

a.lead: **No.** CPU is an **infrastructure metric**.
items: An API can **fail requests or respond slowly while CPU is low**, for example while waiting on a dependency
**Users experience** **latency**, **failure rate** and **uptime**

sub: **Application metrics**: requests per minute, latency, failure rate

a.foot: CPU is still useful for **capacity planning**.

items.label: Retry
items.detail: Retry transient failures with bounded backoff. Repeating writes also requires idempotency or duplicate protection.

items.label: Circuit breaker
items.detail: After repeated failures, calls fail fast instead of piling load onto a broken dependency.

items.label: Bulkhead isolation
items.detail: Separate resources so a slow dependency cannot take down unrelated calls.

items.label: Timeout
items.detail: Do not let a call block a thread indefinitely.

items.label: Fallback
items.detail: Return a default or cached answer when the real call fails.

sections.title: Performance, testing and API architecture maturity
sections.summary: How to make APIs faster and lighter, how to test them beyond functionality, and a seven-level scale of API adoption in an organisation.

items: **Client asks for gzip** → Accept-Encoding: gzip header (and a User-Agent hint)
**Compress** (standard rule) → large text payloads like JSON
**Avoid** → tiny responses or already-compressed content (JPEG, video), where CPU cost outweighs the gain
**Partial response** → returns selected fields to reduce read payloads
**PATCH** → sends a partial update
**Media type and contract** define how fields, parent objects, arrays and removals are applied
**Not always a merge**: do not assume every PATCH is a recursive merge

notes.h: Treat the API as a contract when testing
items: **Check endpoints**
**Object model** reflects resources and types
**No missing or duplicate** functionality
**Resource relationships** are reflected
**Test plans**: manual or automated
**Isolated requests**
**Multi-step workflows**
**Combined UI and API tests**
**Happy-path positive** tests
**Extended positive** with optional parameters
**Negative** with valid or invalid input
**Destructive** tests
notes.foot: Verify **status code, payload, headers, application state** and basic performance.

items: **Performance** → load and stress tests
**Usability**
**Isolated applications**
**Unstructured integrations** → sockets, file sharing, queues
**Component-based** → EJB, CORBA, web services
**Service-oriented** → ESB, SOAP
**Private APIs on microservices** → REST, API gateway, containers
**Open APIs** → API platform, developer portal, WAF
**APIs as business** → service mesh, GraphQL, gRPC

terms.def: Returning only selected fields of a resource to cut payload size.
Load tests expected traffic; stress pushes beyond limits to find breaking point.
Security principle: access is refused unless explicitly granted.

check.q: A tester checks performance by repeatedly sending requests from a manual API client on a laptop, then reports that the API 'handles load fine'. The target is 3 seconds for 90% of requests at 5,000 concurrent users. Do you accept the result?

items: **Manual requests from one laptop** → neither the **target concurrency** nor **repeatable conditions**
→ results vary with the laptop and network and say little about the **90th percentile**
**Fix**: run **automated load and stress tests** that generate the defined **concurrency and duration** from a **controlled environment**
Report **percentile latency** against the target
**Stress tests** then show **where the API breaks** beyond that load

check.q: An API passes all its functional tests and will be public from launch. What else would you check before production?

sub: No **internal data leaking** into public responses

items: **Performance**: **load and stress tests** against the expected traffic
**Usability** for developers
**Monitoring** in place for **latency** and **failure rate**
a.foot: Functional tests show that the **contract works**, not that the API is **safe or fast enough**.

check.q: Average responses are 2 KB of JSON, one report endpoint returns 3 MB of JSON, and the API also serves images. Where would you enable gzip?

a.lead: Enable it for the **large JSON report** and other **big text responses**.
items: There the **bandwidth saved** outweighs the **compression CPU**
**Skip small payloads**: the cost is not worth it
**Skip already-compressed content** such as **images**
a.foot: **Measure** response size and latency **before and after**, rather than turning it on everywhere.

check.q: A mobile list screen downloads full 40-field product objects to display three fields, and an edit screen sends the whole object with PUT to change one price. What would you change in each?

items: **List → partial response**: the server returns **only the requested fields** → cuts **payload** and **parsing time**
**Edit → PATCH** with only the fields to modify, plus any **enclosing parent objects**
a.foot: Two different tools: a **partial response** trims what the **server sends**, and **PATCH** trims what the **client sends**.

layers.label: 7: APIs as business
layers.detail: API platform, service mesh, cloud, GraphQL, gRPC.

layers.label: 6: Open APIs
layers.detail: API platform, developer portal, WAF, REST, OAS.

layers.label: 3: Component-based
layers.detail: EJB, RMI, COM/COM+, CORBA, web services.

layers.label: 2: Unstructured integrations
layers.detail: Sockets, file sharing, message queues, DB replication.

sections.title: OAuth vs JWT vs SAML, CORS and payload inspection
sections.summary: Telling the security standards apart, why browsers need CORS, how to fix CORS errors, and validating requests at the gateway.

items: **OAuth** → authorization framework: a client obtains an access token from a central authorization server
**JWT** → token format (JSON with issuer, subject claims, expiry); can be used inside OAuth; independent of how the token is obtained
**SAML** → Single Sign-On standard; passes identity between sessions using signed XML
**Browsers use server response headers** to decide whether a web page may read a cross-origin API response
**OPTIONS preflight**: some requests first trigger one, for allowed origins, methods and headers
**Does not authenticate** callers
**Does not stop non-browser clients** from reaching the API
**Server policy denies** the domain, scheme, port, header, credential or method
**Server errored** on the pre-flight
**API gateway not relaying** pre-flight responses
**Credentials** (cookies, HTTP auth) were required but not sent
**Content** → validate size or JSON schema against the API schema
**Parameters** → headers, query, path
**Responses** → headers and status codes
**Actions per parameter** → prevent, detect or ignore

terms.def: JSON Web Token: signed JSON carrying claims such as issuer, subject and expiry.
XML-based Single Sign-On standard for exchanging identity between systems.
Browser-enforced response-header policy controlling access to cross-origin responses; some requests require preflight.
Browser's preliminary request asking the server whether the real cross-origin request is allowed.

check.q: Match each need to OAuth, JWT or SAML: (a) a third-party budgeting app needs delegated access to a user's bank transactions; (b) staff already signed in to the corporate portal should reach a partner web app without logging in again; (c) the access token should carry the issuer, subject and expiry in a compact form.

items: **(a) OAuth**: the **authorisation framework** through which the client obtains an **access token** from an **authorisation server**
**(b) SAML**: a **single sign-on** standard that passes identity from an existing session using an **XML document**
**(c) JWT**: a **token format** that can be used inside OAuth
a.foot: A design note saying '**JWT instead of OAuth**' confuses a token format with the framework for obtaining tokens.

check.q: A browser web app gets a CORS error calling your API, but the same request works from a command-line client. What do you check?

a.lead: Check, in order:
items: The server can answer the **pre-flight request** without error
The **API gateway** relays the **pre-flight response** to the browser
a.foot: The command-line client works because **CORS is enforced only by browsers**.

check.q: A teammate proposes a strict CORS policy as the main protection for a payment API. Is that enough?

a.lead: **No.** **CORS** only controls whether a **browser** lets a page from another **origin** read the response.
items: **Scripts, servers** and other **non-browser clients** ignore it entirely
The API must still **authenticate and authorise each call**, **validate payloads** and apply **rate limits**

check.q: Your API receives a million requests a day, 30% of them with missing or null fields, and the application crashes on the nulls. How do you handle this in production?

items: **Validate requests against the API schema at the edge**: content, parameters and headers
**Reject bad ones with a 400** that explains which field is wrong
**Inside the service**: handle optional fields **defensively** → one bad request cannot **crash the process**
**Log and monitor the rejection rate**: **30%** suggests a **client bug** or a **confusing contract** worth fixing at the source

sections.title: API gateway, orchestration and distributed transactions
sections.summary: A gateway simplifies client access; multi-service work still needs explicit handling of partial failures through distributed commit or sagas.

notes.lead: Posed as a question in the lecture.
items: **API gateway** → one entry point
**Handles cross-cutting concerns** → security, routing, aggregation
→ clients are **not coupled** to many services

notes.lead: The API manager calls services in order, e.g.:
items: **Validation service** first
**Service A** next

notes.lead: A million requests a day, 30% with missing or null fields:
items: **Validate input at the edge** → schema validation
**Handle nulls gracefully** rather than crashing

notes.lead: With separate databases, a local transaction cannot atomically update order and inventory together. Options:
items: **Avoid** that requirement
**Distributed commit (2PC)**, where supported
**Eventual consistency and compensation**
**Prepare**: a coordinator asks all participants to prepare
**Commit**: if all report done, it tells them to commit
**Abort**: if one fails, it tells the others to abort
notes.foot: **Strongly consistent**, but couples services and blocks resources.

items: **Services commit local steps**
**Later failure** → business **compensation** for completed steps
**Illustrated event-bus flow**: a central coordinator directs Order and Inventory → **orchestrated**, despite its “choreographer” label
**Choreography** instead → services decide their reactions without a central controller

terms.def: A central manager calls services in a defined order to fulfil one request.
Prepare then commit/abort protocol coordinating atomic commit across participants.
Sequence of local transactions with compensations, coordinated centrally or through services reacting to events.
An action that undoes an earlier completed step when a later step fails.

check.q: An Order service and an Inventory service have separate databases. At peak there are 2,000 orders a minute, and Inventory is sometimes slow. Would you use two-phase commit or a saga?

a.lead: **A saga.**
items: **Two-phase commit** holds **locks across both services** until both are ready → a slow Inventory **stalls every order** and **couples their availability**
**Saga**: each service **commits locally** and **publishes an event**
A failure triggers **compensation**, such as cancelling the order
a.foot: Trade-off: accept **eventual consistency**; must design **compensations** and **idempotent handlers**.

check.q: In the lecture's centrally directed saga, Inventory replies 'Failed to Reserve Items'. What happens next, and why is this orchestration even though messages go through an event bus?

items: **Next**: the **coordinator** sends a **compensating 'Delete Order'** to undo the order already committed, and **notifies the user**
**Orchestration** because **one coordinator decides the next step**; the **event bus is only the transport**
In **choreography**, each service would **react to the failure event on its own**

check.q: A mobile app calls six microservices directly, each with its own address, authentication scheme and response format. What problems does this cause, and what does an API gateway fix?

sub: The app is **coupled** to each service's **location and contract**
→ every internal change risks **breaking a released app**
Can **compose several calls** into one response
Lets services **move or split** behind it

a.foot: Cost: it adds a **hop** and a component that must be **highly available**.

steps.label: Create order
steps.detail: A central coordinator requests order creation; Order saves it locally and reports Order Created.

steps.label: Reserve items
steps.detail: The coordinator requests Inventory to reserve the items.

steps.label: Inventory fails
steps.detail: Inventory reports that it could not reserve the items.

steps.label: Compensate
steps.detail: The coordinator requests Delete Order as compensation and reports failure to the user.

exam_angles.q: A clinic platform's first two APIs are designed as follows. API 1: URI /v2.3/appointments/{patient-id}/book, service BookingManager, input the patient id, output the list of all doctors, HTTP verb GET. API 2: URI /v2.3/appointments/{patient-id}/cancel, service BookingManager, inputs the patient id and patient name, output the list of all patients' appointments, HTTP verb GET. (1) Do they comply with RMM level 2? (2) Propose a versioning strategy that affects consumers less. (3) Give corrected interfaces.

sub: But GET is used for **state-changing actions** and **verbs sit in the path**, so HTTP verbs aren't used as **level 2** requires
Only the **major version** in the URI (/v2) or in a **header**
Keep **minor and patch** releases **backward compatible** → consumers unaffected by them
**Book**: POST /v2/patients/{patient-id}/appointments; inputs doctor id and time slot → **201** + the created appointment with its **location**
**Cancel**: DELETE /v2/patients/{patient-id}/appointments/{appointment-id}, or **PATCH** its status to cancelled → **204** or the updated appointment
Drop the **redundant patient name** and the unrelated lists of **all doctors** or **all appointments**

exam_angles.q: Design a RESTful API for a cleaning-service platform. Customers make one-off orders or subscribe to OnceAFortnight, OnceAWeek or TwiceAWeek plans, change or cancel subscriptions, and pay; the mobile app retries on timeouts. Give resources, verbs and status codes, and explain how you handle retries.

sub: /customers/{customer-id}/orders: **POST** creates a one-off order (**201**); **GET** lists orders with ?status= and **pagination**
/customers/{customer-id}/subscriptions: **POST** subscribes (**201**); **PATCH** /subscriptions/{subscription-id} changes the plan (**200** or **204**); **DELETE** cancels (**204**)

items: **Naming**: plural **kebab-case nouns**, no verbs, **path variables** for identity and **query parameters** for filtering
**Retries**: retried POSTs to orders, subscriptions and payments carry an **idempotency key** → the server returns the **recorded outcome** for a repeat
**Maturity**: aim for **level 2**; add links (**level 3**) such as a subscription's **cancel** and **change-plan** links if clients would benefit
**Versioning**: version as /v1

exam_angles.q: A published API at version 1 has 200 partner integrations. You must split 'name' into 'firstName' and 'lastName', add an optional loyalty-points field, and fix a currency-rounding bug. Plan the releases and the partner impact.

items: **Bug fix → patch**; **optional loyalty field → minor** release: neither breaks partners, so they need **no changes**

items.t: **Name split → version 2** (/v2 or a v2 **media type**)
sub: Changes meaning and **removes a field** → breaking
**Version 1 keeps returning 'name'** under an **explicit service level**

items: **Announce** the change and its **timeline** through the **developer portal**; **track v1 usage per partner** before retiring it
a.foot: Cost: running **two versions side by side** for the migration period.

exam_angles.q: A public payment API serves a browser single-page app and partner servers. It receives a million requests a day, 30% with malformed or null fields, and retried POSTs have caused some duplicate charges. Design its security and robustness, and name one drawback of your design.

sub: **OAuth 2.0 access tokens** (**JWT** is one possible format)
**Schema validation** that rejects malformed requests with a **400**

items: **Services still authorise each action** and validate **business invariants**
Configure **CORS** for the single-page app's **origin only**, remembering that **CORS is not authentication**
Require an **idempotency key** on payment POSTs → retries return the **original result**
Add **timeouts**, **circuit breakers** on downstream calls, and **monitoring** of **latency** and **failure rate**
a.foot: **Drawback**: the gateway is a **critical shared component**, and strict validation will initially **reject many partner requests** until partners fix their clients.

exam_angles.q: After a release, the 95th-percentile latency of GET /orders rose from 300 ms to 4 seconds, while database query times are unchanged. Give the most likely causes, how you would confirm them, a fix, and the fix's drawback.

items.t: **Likely causes**: fast queries → the time is spent elsewhere
sub: A **thread or connection pool** being exhausted
Then check **pool metrics** and the **release diff**

items.t: **Fix** (if a downstream call is the cause)
sub: Add a **timeout** and **circuit breaker** with a **fallback**
Or call it **in parallel**, or **cache** the result

items: **Drawback**: **degraded or slightly stale** responses when the fallback or cache is used → the change needs a **load test** before release

exam_angles.q: A product team must choose between REST and GraphQL for a mobile dashboard that aggregates data from six microservices; a public catalogue endpoint on the same platform is mostly anonymous, repeated reads. Recommend a style for each and give the trade-offs.

sub: **Client-driven**: one query to one endpoint fetches **exactly the fields** needed from several services
The **schema and type system** document the data
Identical repeated reads benefit from ordinary **HTTP and CDN caching**, which GraphQL makes hard

a.foot: Cost: **two styles** to run and secure, plus **resolvers** that must call the six services efficiently.
